query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the build substrate during selective laser melting of high-entropy alloys will decrease fabrication‐induced defects and residual thermal stresses, thereby improving dimensional precision and mechanical integrity compared to components produced under room-temperature substrate conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured high-entropy alloy components (e.g., CoCrFeNiCu or similar HEAs) produced by SLM using standard processing parameters with an unheated (room-temperature) build substrate.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled substrate preheating step during the SLM process by elevating the build platform temperature to a predetermined level, while keeping other laser and scan parameters constant.
generation.conditions: SLM processing performed in an inert atmosphere with identical laser power, scan speed, and hatch spacing for both control and intervention groups; the only variable changed is the substrate temperature, which is actively maintained at a controlled high temperature (value to be optimized based on alloy system) throughout the build.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients during solidification lead to lower residual stresses and smoother interlayer fusion, thereby minimizing pore formation, cracking, and other fabrication-induced defects.
generation.mechanism: Preheating the substrate moderates the cooling rate, reducing thermal shock and rapid solidification. This in turn minimizes the formation of internal stresses and defects, ensuring a more uniform microstructure and improved interlayer bonding, which collectively enhance dimensional accuracy and mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA components fabricated with substrate preheating are expected to demonstrate lower defect densities (e.g., reduced porosity and fewer cracks), superior dimensional precision, and improved mechanical properties (such as increased yield strength and toughness) relative to the baseline fabricated without preheating.
generation.baseline: Components produced via standard SLM without substrate preheating, which typically exhibit higher residual stresses, a greater density of fabrication-induced defects, and lower dimensional accuracy.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be beneficial as long as the preheating temperature is optimized to avoid adverse effects such as excessive grain growth or oxidation; its effectiveness may vary with different HEA compositions and machine-specific parameters.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimum substrate temperature and the quantitative magnitude of improvements in mechanical integrity and dimensional precision are not fully determined and will require experimental optimization tailored to each specific HEA system.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of high-entropy alloy samples using SLM under otherwise identical conditions: one set with standard room-temperature substrate and one set with the controlled preheating intervention. Ensure that the only variable is the substrate temperature. Post-fabrication, assess the dimensional precision using high-resolution metrology and analyze the microstructure for defects using X-ray computed tomography (CT) and electron microscopy. Conduct mechanical tests (e.g., tensile tests) to evaluate differences in yield strength, ductility, and toughness.
measurements: Dimensional accuracy measurements (e.g., using laser scanning or coordinate measuring machines)
Defect density and morphology (via X-ray CT and SEM)
Mechanical properties (tensile strength, yield strength, and elongation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not show a statistically significant decrease in defect density and improvement in dimensional precision and mechanical properties compared to the control samples, or if negative side effects (such as degradation of microstructural features or mechanical performance) are observed, the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study uniquely demonstrates the processability, hot-cracking susceptibility, and in situ mechanical response of CoCrFeNiCu-HEA fabricated by L-PBF, providing new insights into defect evolution and mechanical performance under these specific processing conditions. Future work will focus on targeted alloying (e.g., Al addition), pre-heating strategies, and optimized scanning to further reduce hot-cracking susceptibility and enhance mechanical performance. This study provides insights into the processability, defect evolution, and mechanical response of L-PBF CoCrFeNiCu-HEA, guiding the development of crack-resistant, additively manufactured HEAs.

It has been highlighted that even small changes in processing parameters have a significant effect on the physical properties and microstructure of the final parts [], and even give rise to major defects in the parts, e.g., unreasonable process parameters [], internal defects induced by incomplete laser scanning filling [], geometric defects and macroscopic deformations under residual stress generated by apparent thermal gradients in the manufacturing process [], severe notching or deformation of the support bar. The literature [] illustrates the causes of these defects and concludes that the mechanical and biological properties of the parts are seriously affected. It is also found in the literature [] that the fatigue life of SLMed parts under multi-axle load is significantly reduced due to stress concentration caused by internal defects compared to forgings and that defects also affect the manufacturability, dimensional accuracy and surface roughness of SLM lattice structure [].
